plio-006.title: The oreodonts vanish
plio-006.text: Oreodonts were plant-eating hoofed mammals, and they had stayed diverse ever since the Oligocene, through millions of years of cooling and spreading grass. They had seen the age of the giant Paraceratherium and the rise of the grazing horses. In the earliest Pliocene they disappeared, the end of the decline that began with the turnover described in {{ref:mioc-126}}.

plio-042.title: Australopithecus africanus and the Taung Child
plio-042.text: The Taung Child, a juvenile skull about 2.8 million years old, was the first early hominin ever found. It belongs to Australopithecus africanus, which lived in South Africa from about 3.3 to 2.1 million years ago. Its fossils come from Taung, Sterkfontein, Makapansgat and Gladysvale. It walked well on two legs, though less efficiently than humans, and kept a more apelike upper body than East Africa's A. afarensis. It lived in gallery forest bordered by grassland and ate a highly varied diet, including grasses and seeds. Strong swings in climate probably ended it, perhaps along with competition from Homo and Paranthropus robustus.

plio-048.title: Lucy, the skeleton that walked before it thought big
plio-048.text: Lucy's skeleton is about 40% complete, and it settled an old question. She was a female Australopithecus afarensis who lived at Hadar in Ethiopia's Afar region around 3.2 million years ago. Her skull was small and ape-like, but she walked upright on two legs. So walking upright came before larger brains. Her age is well pinned. Ash layers beneath the fossil were argon-dated to 3.22 and 3.18 Ma, the younger only one metre below her. Nearby, the 'First Family' site AL 333, about 3.2 million years old, holds at least thirteen individuals of different ages.

plio-049.title: The eastern Pacific's permanent El Niño ends
plio-049.text: In the early to mid Pliocene, the eastern equatorial Pacific stayed warm all the time, in a permanent El Niño-like state. The warm water absorbed sunlight and lowered Earth's reflectivity. Around 3 million years ago, cold surface water appeared there. That change may have helped cool the globe. It may also have changed how Earth's climate responded to the slow cycles of its orbit.

plio-050.title: Savannas spread across East Africa
plio-050.text: Around 3 million years ago, as the climate turned cooler and drier, savanna expanded in East Africa. Pliocene cooling may have hastened the loss of forests and the spread of grasslands. Some researchers think the change shaped human evolution. One hypothesis holds that walking upright and other hominin traits evolved as forests opened into savanna. Another links the savanna to fire. Wildfires there were common but easier to survive, and moving into that setting may have been the first step toward early humans' control of fire.

plio-051.title: South America's native predators collapse
plio-051.text: Roughly 3 million years ago, South America's native meat-eaters collapsed, including the last sparassodonts, the continent's meat-eating metatherians, relatives of marsupials. Thylacosmilids last occur about 3 Ma, already rare before the continents met. Terror birds also declined after that. The timing does not fit simple replacement by northern invaders. Dogs and weasels reached South America about 2.9 Ma but stayed rare until the Pleistocene. By the Pliocene only two sparassodont families were left, and hathliacynids are last known from the early Pliocene. Their long decline, from the Late Miocene on, may be linked to cooling and the onset of Quaternary glaciation.

plio-053.title: The South Asian summer monsoon strengthens
plio-053.text: After 2.95 Ma, the South Asian Summer Monsoon grew stronger. The likely cause lay at sea, in the Indonesian Throughflow, the current that carries water from the Pacific to the Indian Ocean between the islands of Indonesia. That flow was reorganized, and the monsoon responded, another sign of how ocean gateways shaped Asia's rains.

plio-054.title: Oldowan tools: the first widespread toolkit
plio-054.text: At Nyayanga on Kenya's Homa Peninsula, the oldest known Oldowan tools date to about 2.9 million years ago. The Oldowan, also called Mode I, was the first widespread stone-tool industry. Hominins across much of Africa used it from about 2.9 Ma until at least 1.7 Ma. Thousands of artifacts at Gona, Ethiopia, are firmly dated to 2.6 Ma. Who made them is uncertain. Tools of about 2.6 Ma at Ledi-Geraru may be the work of early Homo, and Australopithecus garhi is another candidate. The tools served mainly for butchering: 2.5-million-year-old tools lay beside cut-marked bones. Homo habilis made Oldowan tools from about 2.3 Ma.

plio-055.title: The Ledi-Geraru jaw, the first Homo
plio-055.text: A jawbone from Ledi-Geraru in Ethiopia's Afar region, LD 350-1, is the oldest known fossil of the genus Homo. It dates to 2.8-2.75 million years ago. Its age suggests Homo may have evolved from Australopithecus afarensis around then. Homo is assumed to have emerged by about 2.8 Ma, most likely in East Africa's Rift Valley. Teeth from Koobi Fora, Kenya, dated 3-2.7 Ma, may belong to the same species. The origin of Homo coincided with climate changes, but too few fossils are known to say whether climate was the cause.

plio-056.title: The Isthmus of Panama joins the Americas
plio-056.text: Around 2.8 million years ago, a thin strip of land rose between the Americas and changed the oceans of the world. South America became attached to North America through the newly formed Isthmus of Panama. It rose at a convergent plate margin, partly built by volcanoes. The closure was gradual. Surface-water exchange through the seaway may already have been fading by 4.6-4.2 Ma. The closing cut the Caribbean off from Pacific nutrients 4.5-3 Ma. The isthmus closed the last strait outside the polar regions linking the Pacific and Atlantic. It ended the last remnant of a current that had flowed around the equator since the Cretaceous. More heat and salt were pushed toward the North Atlantic. Strengthened Gulf Stream and Humboldt currents cooled the Arctic, eventually leading to the glaciations in {{ref:plio-058}}. On land, it opened the road for the exchange in {{ref:plio-057}}.

plio-057.title: The Great American Interchange
plio-057.text: Cats, condors, raccoons and camelids walked south. Armadillos, hummingbirds and opossums headed north. From around 2.7 million years ago, the new land bridge in {{ref:plio-056}} set off the last and largest wave of migration between the Americas. Ground sloths and glyptodonts reached North America. Xenarthrans, the group of sloths, armadillos and anteaters, were among South America's most successful emigrants. Horses and tapirs entered South America. There, competition from northern hoofed mammals helped push the native ungulates toward extinction. The exchange was lopsided. Extinction rates were much higher in South America, and North American groups diversified greatly in their new home. Crossings had begun earlier, as {{ref:mioc-118}} shows, but the land bridge turned a trickle into a flood.

plio-058.title: Ice spreads across the Northern Hemisphere
plio-058.text: Around 2.7 million years ago temperatures dropped, and glaciation began in the Northern Hemisphere. The evidence lies on the seafloor. Ice-rafted cobbles, dropped by melting icebergs on North Atlantic and North Pacific seabeds, and an abrupt shift in oxygen isotopes mark the new Arctic ice. Greenland's separate ice caps merged into one ice sheet covering most of the island, once carbon dioxide fell to 280-320 ppm, 2.7-2.6 Ma. Several causes are suggested. One is falling carbon dioxide. Another is a stronger North Atlantic circulation after Panama closed, which carried moisture north to feed the ice. A weakening Indonesian Throughflow also cut the heat carried toward Antarctica. As sea levels fell, that cooling fed on itself in a self-reinforcing loop.

plio-059.title: Paranthropus, the robust hominins, appear
plio-059.text: The robust hominin genus Paranthropus evolved around 2.7 million years ago. Its earliest species, P. aethiopicus, lived in East Africa about 2.7-2.3 Ma and is known from Lake Turkana. The oldest remains, from Ethiopia's Omo Kibish Formation, date to 2.6 Ma. The genus was still present at the start of the Pleistocene.

plio-060.title: Supernovae leave iron-60 on the seafloor
plio-060.text: Only supernovae, exploding stars, can make radioactive iron-60. Ancient seabed deposits record a large influx of it about 2.6 million years ago. A scattered excess over 10 million years suggests several fairly close supernovae, perhaps from the passing Scorpius-Centaurus group of young stars. So close an explosion could have damaged Earth's ozone layer and killed some ocean life.

reviews.pliocene-epoch: The Pliocene began warm, with carbon dioxide close to today's level and sea level about 25 m higher at its peak. Then geography turned the dial. The Isthmus of Panama joined the Americas, setting off the Great American Interchange and pushing heat and moisture north, and by 2.7 million years ago ice was spreading across the Northern Hemisphere. Savannas spread across East Africa as the climate dried. On them walked a growing cast of hominins, from Ardi and Lucy to the first Homo, who left footprints at Laetoli and the first stone tools at Lomekwi.
